newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Rich UN agency forced to delay $60 mln HQ plan.
newsitem.headline: Rich UN agency forced to delay $60 mln HQ plan.

text.p: The only profitable U.N. agency, the World Intellectual Property Organisation, on Tuesday shelved a controversial plan to build a new $60 million headquarters in Geneva under U.S. pressure to cut costs, diplomats said.

The budget and premises committee of WIPO, which coordinates patents, trademarks and copyrights, delayed the decision until September's General Assembly meeting in New York when a new director general will be appointed to replace its retiring boss, Arpad Bogsch.

Bogsch, a Hungariaan-born U.S. citizen now in his late 70s who retires late this year, lobbied for the new building and angered Washington, which last year slammed the plan as unacceptable when the United Nations is in financial crisis.
A spokesman at the U.S. mission welcomed the delay and said it would be up to the new WIPO chief to make a decision.
"We think this is a very wise and prudent decision at a time of 20-30 percent vacancy rates in Geneva in terms of commercial office space," he said.
WIPO, which has a 12-storey headquarters in Geneva and also purchased a four-storey adjacent building, wanted a new headquarters built on land being offered by a Swiss firm.
WIPO spokesman Laurent Manderieux told reporters earlier on Tuesday that the cost for the new building was estimated at some 95 million Swiss francs ($63 million).
Sources close to the negotiations said Switzerland had offered to extend a credit to WIPO for it to buy the plot.
WIPO is rare among U.N. agencies because it has a budget surplus and larger financial autonomy.

Unlike many other U.N. agencies, more than 85 percent of its revenues come from companies and not from government contributions. Revenues from 47,000 international patent applications processed in 1996 totalled some $94 million.
Financial reserves from the surplus budget will total $140 million at the end of 1997, spokesman Manderieux said.

In a bid to increase WIPO's autonomy, Bogsch also wants a 50 percent cut in the contributions of member states, which would slash their share in total revenues to below eight percent, or suspend them altogether, WIPO officials said.
